_comment: Decision tree shared by the Python app and the web page. Each option's 'where' is a condition on a vehicle; {} matches everything. Conditions: {field, in|eq|ne|gte|lte|any_of}, or {all: [...]} / {any: [...]}. A missing (null) value never satisfies a condition. 'about' is a short explanation the web page can expand. It is not a filter.

start.prompt: What will you mainly use this vehicle for?

options.label: Commuting and errands
options.about: Sedans, hatchbacks, and wagons. Easy to park, with room for a person or two and some bags.

options.label: Family of up to 5, with room for gear
options.about: Those same cars, plus minivans, which carry people and cargo without being an SUV.

options.label: Carrying 6 or more people
options.about: Minivans, and any other model NHTSA lists with at least 6 seats.

options.label: Towing, hauling, or work
options.about: Pickup trucks. This list does not include an official tow rating.

options.label: Fun / weekend driving
options.about: Coupes and convertibles.

options.label: Not sure, show me everything
options.about: Every body style still in the list. The next question lets you narrow it.

start.about: This chooses a body style. SUVs and crossovers are already left out.

family_body.prompt: Which body style do you prefer?

options.label: Sedan
options.about: A separate trunk. Usually the quietest and cheapest shape of a given car.

options.label: Hatchback
options.about: The cargo area opens with the rear window. Often more room than the sedan of the same car.

options.label: Wagon
options.about: A longer roof and a tall cargo hold. Still a car, not an SUV.

options.label: Minivan
options.about: Sliding doors and three rows. The usual stand-in for a three-row SUV.

options.label: No preference
options.about: Keeps every family body style still available.

family_body.about: These are the family shapes still available. It does not change the powertrain or the price.

body_any.prompt: Any body style you have in mind?

options.label: Sedan
options.about: A separate trunk.

options.label: Hatchback
options.about: A rear hatch, usually with more cargo room than a sedan.

options.label: Wagon
options.about: A long roof and a tall cargo hold.

options.label: Coupe
options.about: Two doors, and usually a lower roof.

options.label: Convertible
options.about: A roof that folds.

options.label: Minivan
options.about: Sliding doors and three rows.

options.label: Pickup truck
options.about: An open bed behind the cab.

options.label: No preference
options.about: Keeps every body style still available.

body_any.about: Every non-SUV shape in the list. Pick one, or keep them all.

cab.prompt: What size cab do you need?

options.label: Crew cab (4 full doors)
options.about: Four full doors and a back seat adults can use.

options.label: Extended cab (small rear seats)
options.about: A smaller back seat, often with half-doors.

options.label: Regular cab (no rear seats)
options.about: One row of seats.

options.label: No preference
options.about: Includes pickups whose cab size was not listed.

cab.about: Cab size is the doors and seats of a pickup. Listings that don't state it only stay if you choose no preference.

options.label: Yes, a convertible
options.about: The roof folds down.

options.label: No, a hardtop coupe
options.about: A fixed roof and two doors.

options.label: Either is fine
options.about: Keeps both coupes and convertibles.

roof.about: A convertible folds the roof. A coupe is the fixed-roof version.

options.label: Yes, I need back seats
options.about: Drops cars EPA calls two-seaters, unless NHTSA lists 4 or more seats.

options.label: No, two seats is fine
options.about: Seat count does not filter the list.

rear_seats.about: Some sports cars seat only two. 'Yes' keeps a car EPA does not call a two-seater, or that NHTSA lists with 4 or more seats.

options.label: Fully electric
options.about: No gas engine. The next question is driving range.

options.label: Hybrid or plug-in hybrid
options.about: A gas engine plus a battery. A plug-in can drive a short distance on electricity alone.

options.label: Any electrified (hybrid, plug-in, EV, fuel cell)
options.about: Hybrid, plug-in, battery-electric, or hydrogen fuel cell.

options.label: Gas or diesel (no electrification)
options.about: No hybrid system and no plug.

options.label: No preference
options.about: Keeps every powertrain still available.

power.about: Taken from the listing's fuel type, and checked against EPA for that model year.

ev_range.prompt: How much EPA-rated range do you need?

options.label: 300+ miles
options.about: The longest EPA ranges. Fewer charging stops on a trip.

options.label: 250+ miles
options.about: Enough for most days, with some highway range to spare.

options.label: 200+ miles
options.about: A full charge covers a long day. Road trips need more planning.

options.label: Any range
options.about: Range does not filter the list.

ev_range.about: Official miles on a full charge, for the longest version of that model year. Cold weather and highway speed shorten it.

options.label: Very: 40+ MPG
options.about: Mostly hybrids, plus a few small gas cars.

options.label: Somewhat: 30+ MPG
options.about: A typical efficient car. Many compacts qualify.

options.label: At least 20 MPG
options.about: Drops only the thirstiest engines.

options.label: Don't care
options.about: Fuel economy does not filter the list.

mpg.about: EPA combined city and highway MPG, using the most efficient version of that model year. A hybrid can set the number even when a gas version is thirstier.

options.label: All-wheel or four-wheel drive
options.about: Power can reach all four wheels. Useful in rain or snow. It usually costs more and uses more fuel.

options.label: Front-wheel drive
options.about: The front wheels pull the car. Common on cars and minivans.

options.label: Rear-wheel drive
options.about: The rear wheels push the car. Common on sports cars and some trucks.

options.label: Any drivetrain
options.about: Drivetrain does not filter the list.

drive.about: Which wheels the engine turns. This is separate from automatic or manual.

price.prompt: What's the most you want a typical used example to cost in California?

options.label: Under $15,000
options.about: Usually an older model year. A nearly new car rarely qualifies.

options.label: Under $25,000
options.about: Recent efficient cars start to appear here.

options.label: Under $40,000
options.about: Covers most non-luxury model years, including many nearly new ones.

options.label: Under $60,000
options.about: Drops only the most expensive model years.

options.label: Any price
options.about: Price does not filter the list.

price.about: The median asking price for that model year among used and certified cars in California. Not a price for one specific car.

year.prompt: How new does it need to be?

options.label: 2022 or newer
options.about: Recent cars. Prices are higher, and mileages are usually lower.

options.label: 2018 or newer
options.about: Drops the oldest cars and still includes many under $25,000.

options.label: 2012 or newer
options.about: Most of the cars in this list from the last decade and a half.

options.label: Any model year
options.about: Model years 2005 through 2026.

year.about: Each model year stays separate, so an older generation can fit a budget without hiding the new one.

fuel_cost.prompt: What's the most you want to spend on fuel in a year?

options.label: Under $1,500
options.about: Mostly hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and electric cars.

options.label: Under $2,000
options.about: Efficient gas cars qualify here too.

options.label: Under $2,500
options.about: Drops the heavier and more powerful engines.

options.label: Any fuel cost
options.about: Yearly fuel cost does not filter the list.

fuel_cost.about: EPA's yearly estimate for the cheapest version, at its standard miles and fuel price. Your bill depends on how far you drive.

mileage.prompt: What's the most mileage you want on a typical example?

options.label: Under 30,000 miles
options.about: Mostly recent model years.

options.label: Under 60,000 miles
options.about: A common line for a used car that is still fairly fresh.

options.label: Under 100,000 miles
options.about: Leaves out the highest-mile examples of older years.

options.label: Any mileage
options.about: Mileage does not filter the list.

mileage.about: The median odometer reading on California listings for that model year. Newer years usually have fewer miles.

options.label: Manual
options.about: You shift gears yourself. Fewer of these are listed.

options.label: Automatic
options.about: The car shifts, or it is electric and has one speed.

options.label: Either
options.about: Includes cars whose transmission was not listed.

transmission.about: Automatic includes CVTs and the single-speed gearboxes in electric cars. A manual has a clutch. Cars with no gearbox listed only stay under Either.

cargo.prompt: How much cargo space do you need?

options.label: A lot: 20+ cubic feet
options.about: Hatchbacks and wagons more often than sedans.

options.label: At least 15 cubic feet
options.about: A normal trunk, or anything larger.

options.label: At least 10 cubic feet
options.about: Drops only the smallest cargo areas EPA measured.

options.label: No preference
options.about: Includes vehicles EPA did not measure, such as many trucks and minivans.

cargo.about: EPA luggage volume for the roomiest version. A sedan trunk is often about 15 cubic feet, and a hatchback often 20 or more. Pickups and minivans are often blank, because EPA does not require the number.

free_text.placeholder: Or type a brand, such as Honda
free_text.about: Matches the start of the make. Chevy, VW, and Mercedes are recognized.

options.label: American brands
options.about: Ford, Chevrolet, GMC, Tesla, Jeep, Ram, and the other U.S.-based companies in this list.

options.label: Japanese brands
options.about: Toyota, Honda, Nissan, Mazda, Subaru, and their luxury brands.

options.label: Korean brands
options.about: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

options.label: European brands
options.about: BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen, Audi, and the other Europe-based companies in this list.

options.label: No preference
options.about: Brand does not filter the list.

brand.about: A country is where the company is based, not where that car was built. A Toyota built in California is still a Japanese brand. You can also type a name.

seats.prompt: How many people does it need to seat?

options.label: 6 or more
options.about: Minivans, or a model NHTSA lists with at least 6 seats.

options.label: 4 or 5 is enough
options.about: A small family. Two-seat sports cars drop out.

options.label: 2 is fine
options.about: Seat count does not filter the list.

seats.about: Seat counts come from NHTSA when they were recorded. A blank count is not guessed. Minivans count as 6 or more. Most cars count as 4 or 5 from the body style.

safety.prompt: What's the minimum NHTSA overall crash-test rating you'd accept?

options.label: 5 stars only
options.about: Only model years where every tested version scored 5 stars.

options.label: 4 stars or better
options.about: 4 or 5 stars. Unrated model years drop out.

options.label: Any, including models NHTSA hasn't rated
options.about: Stars do not filter the list.

safety.about: The stars shown are the lowest score among versions tested that model year. An unrated model fails a minimum. It stays only if you allow unrated models.

adas.prompt: Do you want forward collision warning and lane departure warning as standard?

options.label: Yes, both standard
options.about: Both warnings were standard equipment that model year.

options.label: Not required
options.about: Driver-assist does not filter the list.

adas.about: Collision warning alerts you to a vehicle ahead. Lane warning alerts you when you drift. Standard means every tested version had it, not that it was an option.

recalls.prompt: How much do recalls matter to you?

options.label: Avoid anything with recalls this model year
options.about: Keeps a model year only when NHTSA lists zero recalls.

options.label: No more than 2 recalls
options.about: Zero, one, or two recalls on the NHTSA record.

options.label: Don't care
options.about: Recalls do not filter the list.

recalls.about: Recall counts come from NHTSA's new-car records. The used-car list does not include them, so this question is skipped there. A blank count is not treated as zero.
